coherence.reasons: Both run a clean four-part hierarchy (economics, exit cost, customer evidence, plan) in which the executive summary maps one-to-one to sections and slide titles. X is tight, but its headline figures move between cases: the governing thought gives a $4.75M–5.5M range, the summary and options table lead with the no-migration $5.5M / $3.4M, and the best case (-$4.75M / -$2.65M) sits in sub-bullets and footnotes. Y carries one consistent pair (-$4.75M year one, -$2.65M recurring at the migration ceiling) from summary through bridge, constraints table, options comparison and board asks, with no-migration shown as a labelled variant. Y's sensitivity table and gate thresholds also tie back to the same numbers (the $0.4M Gate 1 threshold equals the break-even with the full envelope spent). Y's 'our starting hypothesis' slide is a slightly awkward insert but does not break the logic.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (retain C, redesign gated on a pilot, fix bundle fill, revisit a 2029 sunset) and both reject immediate exit on contribution, penalties and constraints. Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It compares all four options on time-phased 2027–29 cash (-$8.73M exit vs +$2.37M redesign, downside +$0.40M), separates delayed sunset without redesign from redesign with a sunset gate, and shows no migration rate makes exit pay. It answers the 'redeploy to D' half of the question directly (yes, in sequence) and tests the price-pressure risk (exit breaks even only if C contribution falls about 70%). Its gates have explicit criteria and its contract plan covers consent-based substitution and expiry-aligned terms. X's options table is sound and its 44% payback threshold is useful, but the alternatives are less quantified, the sunset criteria are looser, and the D-versus-C engineering trade-off is only noted as unquantified.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: $3.8M contribution, $0.4M avoidable, -$2.65M recurring and -$4.75M first year at the ceiling, $6.8M break-even D sales, and redesign payback of 0.44 years. X's figures are all correct (51% of shared cost on 18% of sales, 88% stranded, 2.3x cash limit) and it makes few claims beyond the pack. It properly declines to quantify the engineering opportunity cost. Y does far more arithmetic and the figures I checked all hold: operating profit 10.1 → 7.45 / 6.7, reallocated margins 33.7% / 16.8% / 22.3%, calendar-2027 phasing -3.43, downside +0.40, break-even 19% / 31%, post-redesign margin 29.2%. It also logs its assumptions, including that the penalty counts against the $0.9M envelope, which X assumes silently. Y has two mild overreaches: it states as fact that the bundle shortfall is 'caused by A and B', which the pack implies but does not establish, and it offers a $0.25M 'illustrative ceiling' on engineering opportunity cost that is not a true ceiling, despite the pack's warning against inventing such a figure (it is caveated). On balance Y's deeper, verified use of the critical evidence outweighs these, but only modestly given X's cleaner restraint.

revision.reasons: Both reject the CEO's 'drop C on 8% margin' hypothesis for the right reasons: allocation effect, only $0.4M avoidable, negative exit bridge, penalties, confounded renewal gap. Both also keep an appropriately open mind, saying the renewal evidence neither proves nor rules out a C effect and leaving a 2029 sunset testable. X addresses the CEO's claims directly and proposes like-for-like tests. Y reframes the starting hypothesis as its own 'keep C' rather than the CEO's, which is a slight mismatch with the pack. It still dismantles the CEO's logic more thoroughly: under the same ranking logic B becomes the next 'weakest' after reallocation, and the redesign lifts C's reported margin to about 29%, dissolving the ranking. It marks the attrition claim 'unproven' rather than dismissed, and it shows a real update in its own position: 'retain unchanged' fails and is refined to redesign plus service fix. Its Gate 2 states the conditions under which the exit view would be revived.

overall.reasons: Both documents are correct, defensible and avoid all four traps; X is a concise, accurate deck a board could act on. Y better delivers what the committee asked for. It gives the margin-to-avoidable-cost walk, an exit bridge with the penalty separated, and a single time-phased comparison of exit, retain, delayed sunset and redesign. Its contract plan is concrete, the correlation and dashboard tests are explicit, and the sensitivity table shows which unknowns could change the answer. Its quantified gates (pilot saving of at least $0.4M a year; six sunset criteria) and its sequencing of the engineering team give the board decisions it can approve in February. Y's minor overstatements (A/B causation, the illustrative opportunity-cost bound) are flagged as assumptions and do not affect the conclusion.
